title: How to Spot a Lowball Offer
metaTitle: Spotting a Lowball WV Mineral Offer
metaDescription: How to evaluate a West Virginia mineral rights offer for red flags, missing production data, and pressure tactics before you sign anything.
heroLead: The easiest way to tell a fair offer from a weak one is not the dollar figure by itself, it is whether the buyer actually looked at your title and production history before writing that figure down.
intro: West Virginia mineral owners, especially those holding older family interests or fractional shares inherited through an estate, are a frequent target for cold offers that arrive with no context, no explanation, and a short deadline attached. Some of those offers are perfectly legitimate. Others are built on the assumption that an owner will not check the math or ask questions. This guide covers the patterns worth watching for.
None of this is about assuming bad faith from every buyer. It is about knowing what a responsible offer looks like so you can recognize when one is missing the basics.

sections.heading: An offer that never asked for your production history
paragraphs: If a buyer sends a specific dollar figure without ever asking to see your royalty statements, your lease, or your deed, that figure was not built from your actual interest, it was built from a general assumption about your county or a mailing list. A real offer follows some review of your documents, even a light one, because the value of a producing interest depends heavily on decline behavior that cannot be guessed from an address alone.
This does not mean every unsolicited offer is bad, only that an offer made before any documents changed hands should be treated as a conversation starter, not a final number.

sections.heading: Artificial urgency
paragraphs: Language pushing you to sign within a few days, framed as a limited-time opportunity, is a common pressure tactic and rarely reflects how mineral markets actually move. Production, lease terms, and comparable activity in your area do not change meaningfully in the span of a week. A buyer confident in their number should be comfortable giving you time to review the offer, ask questions, or get a second opinion.
If you feel rushed, that alone is worth pausing on, regardless of how the dollar amount looks.

sections.heading: Vague explanation of how the number was reached
paragraphs: Ask directly how an offer was calculated. A reasonable answer references your production trend, comparable lease or sale activity nearby, and the discount applied for the risk profile of the well or play. A vague answer, or one that will not walk through the reasoning at all, suggests either the buyer has not done the work or does not want you to see the assumptions behind the number.

This is also where hedged language matters. A buyer who talks in ranges tied to current activity, rather than promising a fixed guaranteed figure regardless of how production behaves, is generally being straighter with you about how mineral valuation actually works.

sections.heading: Title shortcuts that skip your actual heirship
paragraphs: For owners holding an interest through an unresolved estate or an undivided share among several heirs, watch for a buyer who wants you to sign without addressing the underlying heirship documentation at all, or who suggests you sign for more than your actual share. A legitimate transaction sells exactly the interest you hold and documents how that interest was established, even if it requires an extra curative step like an affidavit of heirship first.

It is also worth being cautious of a buyer who discourages you from involving other heirs entirely, when their input or documentation might actually be needed to confirm the full ownership picture. A straightforward transaction does not need to keep the rest of your family in the dark about basic facts of the estate.

faqs.question: Is a low offer automatically a lowball offer?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Value legitimately varies based on production decline, play position, and title status, so a lower number is not inherently unfair if the buyer can explain the reasoning behind it with reference to your actual interest.

faqs.question: Should I get more than one offer before selling?
faqs.answer: Comparing offers is generally a reasonable step, particularly for a larger or producing interest, since different buyers apply different assumptions and a second opinion can confirm whether a given offer reflects your interest fairly.

faqs.question: What should I do if a buyer will not explain their number?
faqs.answer: Ask again in writing, and if you still do not get a clear answer referencing your production history or comparable activity, treat that as a reason to slow down and consider other options before signing.

faqs.question: Is it normal for an offer to require a deadline?
faqs.answer: Some transactions do have practical timelines tied to closing logistics, but a genuine deadline should be explainable and reasonable, not used to pressure you into skipping a review of the documents or a second opinion.

faqs.question: What if the buyer already knows I hold only a fractional heirship share?
faqs.answer: That is normal and not itself a red flag, since many West Virginia mineral files involve fractional heirs. What matters is whether the offer is priced against your actual documented share and whether the buyer is willing to work through establishing that share properly rather than asking you to sign around it.
